brief.notification_title: GOOGL -13% drags Nasdaq; rotation lifts health care
brief.market_summary: The S&P 500 is barely lower at 7,725.56 (-0.24%), but that small move hides a big rotation. Alphabet is down about 13% and ServiceNow and Fortinet are down more than 20%, dragging the Nasdaq 1.09% lower. Meanwhile the Russell 2000 is up 1.30%, health care (XLV) 1.99%, utilities 1.55% and financials 1.40%, and the VIX is just 16.42. Treasuries are rallying (10Y 4.982%, -6.3bp) even though Q3 GDP grew 3.4% (vs 3.1% expected) and September PCE inflation came in at 3.6% (core 3.1%), both in line. Brent is lower on a reported Vance letter seeking to restart Iran talks; the screen shows 109.70 (-4.87%), which probably includes a contract roll. Bitcoin fell below $80K overnight and has recovered to $81,680 (+1.5%), while most altcoins are still down 15–24% over the past month.
brief.since_last: 1) The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on a 10–2 vote. Cook and Hammack dissented in favour of a hike, and the statement upgraded activity to "strong" (n151). 2) Alphabet badly missed on EPS ($2.12 vs $2.94). Search growth slowed to 12%, free cash flow was -$9.1B, and it kept its spending guidance. The stock fell about 13%, a record loss of roughly $500B (n75, n44). Microsoft beat ($4.89 vs about $4.71–4.73, Azure +48%), and the stock is up about 2.7%. 3) Software sold off hard: NOW -25% and FTNT -21% to -26% (n2, n18). 4) Q3 GDP came in at 3.4%, PCE at 3.6% headline and 3.1% core (both in line), and jobless claims at 194K (n61). Yields still fell about 6bp. 5) The ECB held at 2.5%; markets read it as a hawkish pause and price 67% odds of a December hike. Lagarde will leave on Feb 7 (n35). 6) Oil fell on a reported Vance letter to Iran (n180). Shell and TotalEnergies roughly doubled profits on record refining margins (n124, n143). 7) LLY and MRK beat and raised guidance; CAT fell about 12% after keeping, not raising, its guidance.

economic_data.takeaway: A clear beat, with business investment +12.7% and consumer spending +3.8%. That supports the Fed's 'strong' wording and its bias to hike, which should push front-end yields up. Yields fell anyway, which tells you today's bond move is about flows out of mega-cap tech, not about growth.
Inflation is still speeding up, but it wasn't worse than feared, so bonds rallied in relief. Much of the gain came from gasoline and transport (n23), which ties the inflation outlook to oil.
Underlying inflation is still rising and well above target. Nothing here argues for cuts, and the hawkish dissenters have cover to keep pushing for a hike.

Flat real spending means households paid more for fuel without buying more. This is the first sign high energy prices are squeezing volumes, and it's a quiet negative for consumer discretionary stocks.
The labour market is tight. Taken with the GDP beat, there is no growth scare to justify buying long bonds.

economic_data.actual: Held at 3.75–4.00% (10–2, two dissents for a hike)
economic_data.takeaway: This was a hawkish hold. Two hike dissents, including Cook's first, tell you the next move is more likely up than down, which keeps T-bill yields around 4% and supports holding cash.
A big upside surprise. Sentiment is strong even though real spending is flat.
The signals are mixed. The crude and distillate draws support prices and refining margins, but the gasoline build alongside flat real spending suggests demand at the pump is fading (n115).
A hawkish pause, with 67% odds of a December hike. Rising policy rates abroad limit how far US long yields can fall.

Wednesday's 5-year auction cleared at 4.708%, well below the prior 5.033%. A weak 7-year result after today's rally would show demand doesn't hold at lower yields, and the 10-year would likely move back above 5%.
A hawkish surprise would add to global term-premium pressure. Japanese investors have already sold foreign bonds for six straight weeks (n162).
This is the wage piece of the hike debate. A reading of 1.0% or higher would give the hawks a third argument after GDP and PCE.

earnings.result: EPS $2.12 vs $2.94 est (-27.9%). Revenue missed (exact figure not found). Search growth slowed to 12% from 17%. Cloud +103% to $30.7B. Capex $51.4B, free cash flow -$9.1B, and spending guidance kept.
earnings.takeaway: Down about 13%, its worst post-earnings drop on record. The market is now judging AI spenders on free cash flow, not just growth. Because spending guidance was kept, chip suppliers' revenue is intact for now, but the pressure on returns is the longer-term threat to semis.

earnings.result: EPS $4.89 vs about $4.71–4.73. Revenue $92.28B vs $90.69B. Azure +48% in constant currency vs a 44–45% guide.
earnings.takeaway: Up about 2.7%. It shows AI demand turning into revenue where the business model can absorb the spending. It's the counterweight to GOOGL in the Nasdaq.

earnings.result: EPS $0.51 vs $0.56 (-8.9%) and a weak outlook.
earnings.takeaway: Down about 25%, its worst day ever (n2). Fears that AI will disrupt seat-based software are now showing up in guidance, not just commentary. I'd avoid software ETFs until that settles.

earnings.result: EPS $0.86 vs $0.77 (+11.7%), but it cut its service-revenue forecast and gross margin fell short.
earnings.takeaway: Down 21–26% despite the EPS beat. In software right now, guidance matters far more than the quarter just reported.

earnings.result: Adj. EPS $7.48 vs $5.38 calendar est (about $6.26–6.35 per other sources). 2026 revenue guidance raised to $91–92B.
earnings.takeaway: Up 4–9%. A large beat with a guidance raise is exactly the kind of upward earnings revision that drives XLV, which is up 1.99% today.

earnings.result: Adj. EPS $2.49 vs $2.09–2.12. 2026 EPS guidance raised to $2.77–2.82.
earnings.takeaway: Up about 5%. A second large-cap pharma beat-and-raise makes the health care rotation look broader than one stock.

earnings.result: Adj. EPS $7.20 vs $7.12. Revenue $20.68B. Full-year guidance kept, not raised.
earnings.takeaway: Down as much as 12%, its biggest drop in years (n19), and a drag on the Dow. When a stock is priced for a raise, merely keeping guidance gets punished. XLI is still up 1.00%.

earnings.result: Adj. EPS $5.31 vs $5.14. Revenue $9.8B (+14%) vs about $9.63B.
earnings.takeaway: Share reaction not confirmed. A solid beat that fits with nominal consumer spending holding up, and XLF is up 1.40%.

earnings.result: Adjusted earnings about $10.8B, nearly double a year ago (calendar est EPS $3.54). Record refining margins and a $5B buyback.
earnings.takeaway: Up about 4%. Together with TotalEnergies ($9.1B, also doubled), it sets up a favourable profit backdrop for XOM and CVX tomorrow and supports the XLE add.

earnings.result: Bar: EPS $2.01 calendar (about $1.97 elsewhere), revenue about $202.2B, AWS about $45.5B.
earnings.takeaway: This is the gate for the next SMH tranche. AWS growth plus capex guidance will tell us whether the market rewards AI spending (like MSFT) or punishes it (like GOOGL).

earnings.result: Bar: INTC EPS $0.28 (vs $0.11 a year ago); SNDK EPS $46.19 (vs $0.90).
earnings.takeaway: SNDK is a direct read on the memory upcycle behind the SMH thesis. Expectations near $46 are very high.
These decide whether to add the second half of XLE. Watch buyback pace and refining commentary in light of Shell's record margins.
These confirm or undercut the health care beat-and-raise pattern behind today's XLV idea.

brief.instructor_take: Don't let the flat S&P fool you. Today is a rotation, not a risk-off day. Nasdaq is down 1.1% on Alphabet and software, while small caps, health care, financials and utilities are up 1–2% and the VIX has fallen to 16.4. The real signal is that the market has started grading AI spenders on free cash flow. Alphabet kept spending and burned $9.1B, and it lost $500B in a day; Microsoft showed Azure revenue up 48% and was rewarded. That matters for semis in two ways. In the short run, spending guidance that holds is chip revenue, which is why SMH is barely down. In the long run, the selling is investors starting to demand capex discipline, and that is the real threat to the chip trade. In bonds, a less experienced investor might see the 10-year back under 5% and buy duration. I wouldn't. GDP was 3.4%, inflation is speeding up to 3.6%, claims are 194K, two Fed officials voted to hike, and the ECB is leaning toward a hike. This rally is relief and money leaving tech, and it faces the 7-year auction today and the ECI tomorrow. My positioning: keep cash in bills, lean into sectors where earnings forecasts are rising (health care after LLY and MRK, energy after Shell and Total), and make tonight's Amazon report the gate for any more semis. I'm leaving crypto alone until Friday's options expiry clears and altcoins stop bleeding. What would change my mind on this defensive tilt: AMZN rewarded for its spending tonight and a calm BOJ, which together would bring tech leadership back fast.

top_ideas.title: Health care: follow the beat-and-raise revisions
top_ideas.one_liner: LLY and MRK beat and raised; stage into XLV before Friday pharma
top_ideas.thesis: Health care is where earnings forecasts are rising right now: Lilly ($7.48 vs about $6.3, revenue guidance raised to $91–92B) and Merck ($2.49 vs $2.09, guidance raised) both beat and raised. The sector also isn't tied to the AI-spending debate that is hitting tech. Money rotating out of mega-cap tech gives it a flow tailwind, and ABBV, AZN and REGN report Friday.
top_ideas.reasoning: The concept I'm applying is earnings revisions. Stocks follow changes in expected profits more reliably than they follow stories. Today two of the largest health care companies raised full-year guidance, while tech's leaders are being judged on cash burn. That gap is why XLV is up 1.99% while XLK is down 0.87%. I'd use XLV rather than LLY because LLY just gapped up 4–9% on one report; the ETF gives me the sector trend without single-stock risk after a big move. What a less experienced investor might miss is that XLV is already up 8.84% in a month, so this isn't an early entry. That's why I buy half now and want a pullback or Friday's reports for the rest. If ABBV and AZN disappoint tomorrow, or XLV gives back today's gap and closes below $176, the theme isn't broad enough and I'm out.

top_ideas.title: XLE: hold half, add after XOM/CVX confirm
top_ideas.one_liner: Shell and Total doubled profits; add XLE's 2nd half if XOM/CVX beat
top_ideas.thesis: Record refining margins doubled profits at Shell ($10.8B, $5B buyback) and TotalEnergies ($9.1B), which sets up well for XOM and CVX on Friday. XLE held up (-0.2%) on a day oil fell, showing the stocks already price in lower crude. The add still waits for confirmation because peace-talk headlines are live.
top_ideas.reasoning: I keep the plan from yesterday, with one point clearer now. The profit driver is refining margins and buybacks, not just the crude price, and that's why I'd own it through XLE rather than BNO. The Shell and Total results show the cash is real. XLE barely moved while front-month Brent fell, which tells me the stocks price in much lower oil than the screen shows. Owning futures through BNO would take on the full binary peace risk, plus contract-roll costs. The thing to watch is the reported Vance letter to Iran (n180). A letter isn't a deal, but it's the path to my invalidation, so I want XOM and CVX to prove themselves before adding. A beginner might see 109.70 (-4.87%) on the screen and panic. That print probably reflects the December-to-January roll, since BNO is only down 0.64%. Use the January contract as the reference for the $105 test from now on.

top_ideas.title: SMH: next tranche waits for Amazon's capex
top_ideas.one_liner: Semis held up as GOOGL fell; Amazon tonight gates the next SMH tranche
top_ideas.thesis: Alphabet kept its spending guidance and Microsoft's Azure grew 48%, so the chip demand behind the memory upcycle is intact. SMH is only -0.37% on a day Nasdaq is down 1.1%. But the market now punishes cash-burning AI spending, so I'm moving the second tranche until after Amazon reports tonight instead of adding before it.
top_ideas.reasoning: Yesterday's rule said add the second third today if MSFT and GOOGL kept or raised capex. Technically that happened, but the market's reaction told me something new: it is punishing big AI spending that doesn't produce cash. This is the instructor's point about pre-set rules. You can tighten entries when new information raises event risk, but you never loosen the invalidation. Amazon is the next big spender to report, within hours, and waiting one night costs little compared with buying right before a binary event. If AWS meets the roughly $45.5B bar and capex is kept or raised, and SMH holds above $550, I add the second third Friday. The last third waits for AMD on Nov 3. Sandisk tonight (EPS bar $46.19) is a direct read on memory pricing. If it disappoints along with a weak AMZN report, I stop adding. One caution: the calendar shows SK hynix missing its EPS estimate ($3.84 vs $5.96), but the stock's reaction this week was positive, so I treat that number as suspect rather than as evidence.

lesson.concept: Free cash flow vs. earnings: the market's scorecard for capex
lesson.explanation: Earnings spread the cost of a data centre over many years through depreciation. Free cash flow is the cash from operations minus the capex actually paid out this quarter. When a company spends heavily, its earnings can look fine while its cash runs out the door. Investors tolerate that while they believe the spending will earn high returns, and they turn on it abruptly when the payback looks less certain or rates make waiting more expensive. That turn is a shift in how the market values the whole AI build-out, not just one stock's bad day.
lesson.todays_example: Alphabet kept its spending guidance, spent $51.4B in capex and reported free cash flow of -$9.1B while search growth slowed to 12%. The stock fell about 13%. Microsoft also spends heavily, but Azure grew 48%, visibly turning spending into revenue, and the stock rose about 2.7%. Fed Chair Warsh's line that 'interest rates get in the cracks' (n108, n147) explains why this scrutiny gets sharper with the 10-year near 5%.
